                            POST-HEARING JOINT REPLY BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
           Covert DCC Ranches LP #1 and #2 (collectively “Covert”), Party 485, and Rodger and

Barbara Maddox (collectively “Maddox”), Party 544, submit this Joint Initial Post-Hearing Reply

Brief and submit the following:

                       I.      INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF REPLY

           This case feels akin to the Hunger Games – pitting hundreds, if not thousands, of

landowners against one another in a designated study area including 6,267 square miles, 1 with 5

different path corridors, 122 identified routes, and 171 links. The Applicants, in their role similar

to the Game Master, laid out the groundwork including hurdles for the skirmishes to begin. And,

although there are numerous issues in this proceeding, the routing issue to decide where to place



1
    Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 4 (Direct Testimony and exhibits of Russell Marusak) at 11.
                                                        1
 and locate of the 765kV transmission line project on a 200-foot easement with tower structures up

to 198 feet tall and 140 feet wide over undisturbed and disturbed property, naturally caused

impacted landowners to rebel and to fight one another to keep the transmission lines off of their

land. Most landowners who participated in this exercise, including the Coverts and Maddoxes,

provided first-hand knowledge and facts about their land, its uses, the delicacies and ecosystems

to be protected, and the meaning and purpose of the land, while often urging that individual links

to be avoided in any route approved in this case. Some landowners retained consultants to muster

some support to avoid placing the lines on their land. These consultants used mathematical tools

or systems, standard deviation tools, or normalized scoring tools that remarkably, but not

surprisingly, always resulted in route recommendations that avoided their respective clients’

property. It is not surprising because each of the analyses focus on specific factors that result in

recalibrating the weight given for a particular factor or set of factors, thereby skewing the outcome

in a manner that ensures that the alternative proposed routes do not cross their clients’ land. The

Coverts and Maddoxes respect the effort, but not the results. Moreover, the Coverts and Maddoxes

understand that this is what happens in a transmission line case with alternative routes. But never

has a transmission line impacted hundreds, if not thousands of landowners and their properties and

never has the PUC had to grapple with such divergent proposals of how to identify the route that

will least impact landowners.

           The Hunger Games always has a twist – something unexpected – thrown in by the Game

Master. In this case, in their Post-Hearing Brief, Applicants listed nine (9) routes that “emerged

as routes of interest at the Hearing”: 894, 891, 572, 487. 410, 392, 296, Cherokee Creek G

(“CCG”), and 894 Western Mod 1. 2 And, the twist was that then Applicants fell short of any



2
    Applicants’ Initial Post-Hearing Brief (Item 6311) at 42.
                                                            2
 substantive analysis of the routes, including its own Best Meets Route, and apparently removed

itself from the routing battle. Instead, the Applicants basically said – whatever route the Public

Utility Commission (“PUC”) ultimately decides, we will build it. It isn’t clear why the Applicants

took this path – but they clearly stepped out of the routing fray. Some will likely contend that the

Applicants’ lack of position on the route means they abandoned the Best Meets Route 894. The

Coverts and Maddoxes disagree. It simply means that the Applicants are willing to stand back and

let the landowners to fight amongst each other and let the ALJs and ultimately the PUC to decide.

        The Coverts and Maddoxes will make it simple for the record. They support and do not

object to Routes 894 3, 891 4, 487 5, 410 6, 392 7, and 894 Western Mod 1. 8 They object to and do

not support Routes CCG, 572, and 296. These three alternative routes move the transmission line

to the most southern corridor of the study area only to avoid the transmission lines crossing certain

landowner properties under the guise of result-oriented analyses. These routes unnecessarily cross

the Coverts and Maddoxes working ranches and homesteads and should be rejected as viable

alternatives.

            II.      ROUTES OF INTEREST THAT SHOULD BE RECOMMENDED
                                       OR ADOPTED

        Of the “routes of interests”, the Coverts and Maddoxes support and do not object to Routes

894, 891, 487, 410, 392, and 894 Western Mod 1. None of these routes include or use Links J33,

J6, or K41. As explained in undisputed testimony and in their Joint Initial Brief, these three links,

4
  Sneed Ex. 2 (Direct Testimony of Karn Smith Hubbard on Behalf of Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed) at 4.
5
  PUC Staff Ex. 1 (Direct Testimony of John Pool, P.E.) at 19.
6
  This route appears to be supported by the K13/K51 Landowners if the ALJs or PUC choose to use a route in the
northern corridor. Initial Post-Hearing Brief of the Segment K13/K51 Landowners at 8 (Item 6256).
7
  Initial Brief of the Brady Creek Intervenors at 28-44 (Item 6280).
8
  This route is an RFI Route proffered by the Link R1 Opposition Landowners. Initial Brief of Link R1 Opposition
Landowners at 20 (Item 6285).
                                                       3
 taken individually or used in combination in any route, do not meet the statutory requirements of

PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(“PUC Rule). 9 Placement of

the project using any of these links will significantly and permanently harm the Coverts’ and the

Maddoxes’ respective land, ranching and hunting operations, native wildlife and vegetation,

aesthetics, and waterways and water sheds. 10

        The Coverts and Maddoxes particularly support Route 894 because it remains the only end-

to-end holistic analysis of route and link alternatives. 11          While some will likely argue that the

Applicants abandoned or no longer support Route 894, the Coverts and Maddoxes disagree. It is

clear that the Applicants intentionally decided to step away from the routing fray to let landowners

duke it out – they no longer want to engage in the fray. And for whatever reason they chose to do

so, it does not affect the weight to be given to the scores of testimonies and evidence submitted by

the Applicants and affected landowners in this record that explains why Route 894 is the Best-

Meets route.

        As informal alliances formed in the Hunger Games, so do they in this proceeding. The

Coverts and Maddoxes concur with and support the following landowners in their analysis

endorsing Route 894: J6, K41, and J33, and K41 Landowner Group, 12 Newman Group, 13 and John

D. Harkey, Jr., The Mason Trust, Black Jack Ranch Trust, and Harkey Ranch Enterprises, Inc.

(collectively “Harkey Ranch”). 14          Avoidance of these three links minimizes the impact on

habitable structures, best protects community values and current uses of the properties, avoids

10
   Id.
11

12

13

14

at Bates Stamp 005-009 (Item 6249).
                                                        4
 multiple lines on the Covert ranches and cutting the Covert ranches in half, and avoids any adverse

park or recreational areas. As noted, however, the Coverts and Maddoxes do not oppose and could

support Routes 487, 891, 410, 392 and 894 Western Mod 1 for the same reasons given by their

respective sponsors.

              III.     OPPOSED ROUTES OF INTEREST THAT SHOULD NOT BE
                                 RECOMMENDED OR ADOPTED

         Routes 572, 296 and CCG are problematic from the outset and should not be recommended

to or approved by the PUC.                 In contrast to the holistic approach based on an extensive

environmental assessment, these three alternative routes are supported by analyses with an agenda

– to avoid their clients’ properties. Regardless of how the analysis was performed, the outputs of

the analysis always resulted in recommended routes that avoided the consultant’s clients’ property.

         Route CCG

         The Coverts and Maddoxes will not repeat the shortcomings of CCG outlined in their Initial

Brief. 15 CCG includes use of Links J33 and J6 – both of which impact and cut through the Coverts

and Maddoxes ranches. 16 Ms. Reinecke’s analysis falls short on several levels. 17 But most

importantly, her analysis is result-driven; it is used to justify how to avoid her clients’ properties

by weighing only certain factors that skew the analysis away from certain areas. It is not a holistic

or independent evaluation – it is simply a means to an end. The PUC has not adopted Ms.

Reinecke’s approach in other transmission line cases and there is nothing in the record that would

suggest her approach and conclusions should be adopted. Other landowners who cite CCG as an

alternative route do not make Ms. Reinecke’s analysis more plausible or credible. Route CCG

should be rejected.


15
   Covert/Maddox Initial Brief at 14-16.
16
   Id.
17
   Id.
                                                        5
         Routes 572 and 296

        Routes 572 and 296 should not be recommended or adopted. They, too, suffer from many

of the same shortcomings found with the Route CCG. Importantly, the analysis also appears to be

result-driven. Mr. Aaron Brewer offered a mathematical analysis of the routes using a normalized

scoring tool. 18 His analysis and explanations focus primarily on Route 572. 19 He adds Route 296

only on the basis of it being “more cost-competitive” than Route 894. 20 And, in its Initial Brief,

Save The Lampasas (“STL”) groups these two routes interchangeably. 21 The ALJs should reject

both routes because:

      1. Mr. Brewer’s scoring tool to support Route 572 has not been adopted by the PUC in any
         prior routing cases. 22

      2. The scoring tool and final analysis is clearly result driven. For example, Mr. Brewer’s
         environmental evaluation is based on the Applicants’ Environmental Assessment and
         Alternate Route Analysis (“EAARA”), Table 7-2 that lists all of the factors assessed.23
         But when Mr. Brewer conducted his mathematical analysis, he did not independently
         recalculate any of the environmental measures in the EAARA Table 7-2 for all routes.24
         For example, he criticized the EAARA for not accounting for the golden cheeked
         warbler. 25 But in his analysis, he made adjustments to account for that issue only on
         routes impacted by Links G51 and G52. 26 The same is true for his criticism related to
         habitable structures – his adjustment only related to property impacted by Links G51 and
         G52. 27

      3. In his mathematical tool analysis, Mr. Brewer adjusted for certain other factors, including
         visual impacts and ranch operations. But his adjustments were only for routes that
         included Links G51 and G52. 28

interchangeably.

       4. He added costs to his analysis only after he completed his scoring analysis and costs were
         treated separately for his analysis. 29


      5. Route 572 is inferior to Route 894 on key factors, including:
            • Route 572 is longer than Route 894. 30
            • Route 572 is more expensive than Route 894. 31
            • Route 572 crosses 45 more streams than Route 894. 32

      6. Route 296 is not the PUC Staff’s “Alternative Route.” Mr. Poole did not recommend
         Route 296 33, although he looked at the route during his initial analysis leading up to the
         filing of his direct testimony. He admitted during the Hearing on the Merits that he would
         want to look at the additional information to reevaluate this route. 34

        Finally, STL highlights the number of participants in its group 35 and cites past PUC

findings about the importance of the Lampasas River valley area 36 in an effort to suggest that their

interests should be given greater weight in this record. Neither the Coverts nor the Maddoxes seek

to minimize the historic work done by STL in transmission line proceedings. However, in this

case, the Coverts and Maddoxes respectfully disagree with any approach that would give STL’s

voice more weight simply because of their participant numbers or past efforts before the PUC.

        First, a larger group of voices does not equate to giving more weight or credibility to that

group’s opinions – particularly if the basic mathematical took is result-driven. STL appears to

have banded together since at least 2009 and encompasses both urban, suburban, and rural areas.

Given the population is denser in the Lampasas area than other areas within the study area in this

proceeding, it makes sense that there will be more involved participants. The Lampasas areas have


29
   Id. at 129:20-25 (Brewer).
30
   Id. at 144:8-10 (Brewer).
31
   Id. at 144:10-12 (Brewer).
32
   Id. at 145:5-16. The increased streams include the creeks and streams located on the Coverts’ ranches and the
Maddox ranches. Covert DCC 1 & 2 Ex. 1 (Direct Testimony of Danay Cottingham Covert) at 7-8; Maddox Ex. 1
(Direct Testimony of Barbara Maddox on Behalf of Rodger and Barbara Maddox) at 6.

   Tr. 75:23-24 (Poole)(June 10, 2026).
34
   Id. at 82:4-9 (Poole).

 had to fight these transmission lines cases before – unlike most of the landowners in this

proceeding who have not, including the Coverts and Maddoxes. But sheer numbers within a group

or their ability to organize participants are not grounds to elevate their positions over the voices

and concerns by hundreds of other landowners.

           Second, the PUC “precedent” cited by STL has limited value in this case. STL cites the

PUC’s findings made in 2010 about the Lampasas River valley in Docket No. 37463. 37 While not

disputing the accuracy of the findings based on that record, the Coverts and Maddoxes submit that

Docket No. 37463 was a relatively small skirmish compared to the expansive study area and

number of potentially impact landowners in this proceeding. That docket impacted landowners

within three counties with the primary focus on the impact of the transmission line on the Lampasas

River Valley. Understandably, then, the PUC would have specific findings about the Lampasas

River Valley to align with the scope of that case. In sharp contrast, this case is far more expansive

in its study area and impact on hundreds of landowners.            Accordingly, in this case, the

determination of Community Values must be based on the evidence in this record and should not

rely on prior findings in a more limited scoped proceeding.

                         IV.    CONCLUSION AND REQUESTED RELIEF

           In the Hunger Games – there were no real winners – even the two triumphant tributes paid

a huge price to be on top. This case is no different because there is no clear cut route or sets of

routes that will not have some impact on landowners. In this case, there are only two routes that

are supported by an end-to-end holistic approach not driven by a pre-determined result: Routes

894 and 478. All other routes supported by landowners using mathematical or statistical

approaches are less credible because they were result-driven. And, in the event, the ALJs



37
     Brief at 12-13.
                                                  8
 determine that a route other than 894 and 478 should be considered, the Coverts and Maddoxes

implore the ALJs to avoid any route that includes Links J33, J6 or K41.
